use: On its own it sounds blunt about a specific man; otoko no hito is the neutral way to say 'a man'.

example.romaji: Otoko tte hontou ni baka da yo ne.
example.ja: 男って本当にバカだよね。
example.english: Men are so dumb, aren't they?

examplePolite.romaji: Otoko tte hontou ni baka desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 男って本当にバカですよね。
examplePolite.english: Men are so dumb, aren't they?

notes: otoko no ko is a boy. Opposite: onna.

use: On its own it sounds blunt, even rude, about a specific woman; onna no hito is the neutral way to say 'a woman'.

example.english: Women are hard to figure out.

examplePolite.english: Women are hard to figure out, aren't they?

notes: onna no ko is a girl. Opposite: otoko.

use: Stresses being human or what kind of person someone is; for 'a person' in daily talk, hito is the usual word.

example.romaji: Ningen dakara, machigai mo aru yo.
example.ja: 人間だから、間違いもあるよ。

examplePolite.romaji: Ningen desu kara, machigai mo arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 人間ですから、間違いもありますよ。

notes: ningen kankei: relationships with the people around you, at work or school.

use: The polite, neutral word for a woman, common in news, shops and whenever you want to sound respectful.

example.romaji: Ano josei, dare da ka shitteru?
example.ja: あの女性、誰だか知ってる？
example.english: Do you know who that woman is?

examplePolite.romaji: Ano josei, dare da ka shitte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの女性、誰だか知っていますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you know who that woman is?

notes: The male counterpart is dansei. Softer than onna.

use: Also a title for doctors, lawyers and writers, used alone or after a name: Tanaka-sensei.

examplePolite.ja: 先生に聞いてみましょう。

use: Anyone who joined your school, club or company before you; used as a name, alone or after a surname.

example.ja: 先輩にご飯おごってもらった。

examplePolite.romaji: Senpai ni gohan o ogotte moraimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 先輩にご飯をおごってもらいました。

notes: Opposite: kouhai (junior). You usually speak to a senpai in desu/masu.

use: Someone you know but aren't close to.

examplePolite.romaji: Ano hito, shiriai na n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの人、知り合いなんですか？

notes: A friend is tomodachi. shiriai ni naru: get to know someone.

use: People on the same side: a team, a crew, a close group of friends.

example.romaji: Minna daiji na nakama da yo.
example.ja: みんな大事な仲間だよ。
example.english: They're all friends who matter to me.

examplePolite.ja: みんな大事な仲間です。
examplePolite.english: They're all friends who matter to me.

notes: Warmer and more group-minded than tomodachi.

use: Every single member of a set group, like a class, team or family.

example.ja: じゃあ、全員そろったから始めよう。
example.english: OK, everyone's here, so let's start.

examplePolite.ja: では、全員そろいましたので始めましょう。
examplePolite.english: Well, everyone's here, so let's begin.

notes: minna is the casual 'everyone'; zen'in stresses that nobody is left out.

use: Often goes straight before a verb with no particle: otagai ganbarou.

example.romaji: Kore kara mo otagai ganbarou ne.
example.ja: これからもお互い頑張ろうね。

examplePolite.ja: これからもお互い頑張りましょう。

notes: otagaisama: 'we're in the same boat', said back when someone thanks or apologises.

use: Making sure something is right or as planned: times, details, bookings.

example.ja: ちょっと確認してくるね。

examplePolite.ja: ちょっと確認してきます。

notes: Also a noun: kakunin ga toreta (it's been confirmed).

use: Finding out something you don't know: online, in a dictionary, or by digging into it.

example.ja: ネットで調べてみるよ。

examplePolite.ja: ネットで調べてみます。

notes: kakunin suru checks what you already think; shiraberu finds out something new.

use: Quick, casual checking of messages, mistakes or a list; also keeping an eye on something.

example.ja: 今朝のメール、チェックした？
example.english: Did you check this morning's email?

examplePolite.romaji: Kesa no meeru wa chekku shimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今朝のメールはチェックしましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you check this morning's email?

notes: Not for paying the bill; that's okaikei.

use: Seeing or trying it yourself to be sure something is true.

example.ja: 自分の目で確かめたい。
example.english: I want to see it for myself.

examplePolite.romaji: Jibun no me de tashikametai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 自分の目で確かめたいです。
examplePolite.english: I want to see it for myself.

notes: Also for feelings: kimochi o tashikameru (find out how someone really feels).

use: X to Y o kuraberu (compare X and Y); X ni kurabete (compared with X).

example.romaji: Hoka no mise to kurabete mita?
example.ja: ほかの店と比べてみた？
example.english: Did you compare it with other shops?

examplePolite.romaji: Hoka no mise to kurabete mimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: ほかの店と比べてみましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you compare it with other shops?

notes: hito to kurabenai de (don't compare yourself with others) is common advice.

use: Mostly as machigatteru or machigatta: it's wrong, you got it wrong.

example.ja: それ、ちょっと間違ってるよ。

examplePolite.ja: それ、少し間違っていますよ。

notes: To mix one thing up with another, use machigaeru: michi o machigaeta (I took a wrong turn). Noun: machigai.

use: Small slips, mainly at work, in games or in sport.

example.ja: ごめん、またミスしちゃった。

examplePolite.ja: すみません、またミスしてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I made another mistake.

notes: Also a noun: ore no misu da (my mistake).

use: Doing something over from the start, from homework to a relationship.

example.ja: だめだ、もう一回やり直そう。
example.english: No good. Let's do it over.

examplePolite.romaji: Dame desu ne, mou ikkai yarinaoshimashou.
examplePolite.ja: だめですね、もう一回やり直しましょう。
examplePolite.english: That's no good. Let's do it over.

notes: -naosu after a verb stem means 'redo': kakinaosu (rewrite), minaosu (look again).

use: Missing something you meant to see, or letting someone off.

example.ja: 昨日のドラマ、見逃した。

examplePolite.ja: 昨日のドラマを見逃しました。

notes: kondo dake minogashite: 'let it slide just this once'.
